content: Lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide are medications used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension). Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, such as strokes and heart attacks. These benefits have been demonstrated in clinical trials across various classes of antihypertensive drugs, including this combination. The combination of lisinopril, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, and hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretic, is not recommended as initial therapy. It is typically used when monotherapy with either component fails to achieve the desired blood pressure control. The combination may also blunt the potassium loss typically caused by diuretics. Patients with severe renal impairment should not use this combination, as thiazides are less effective in such cases, and loop diuretics are preferred. Additionally, this combination is contraindicated in patients with a history of angioedema related to ACE inhibitors, hereditary or idiopathic angioedema, or hypersensitivity to sulfonamide-derived drugs. ACE inhibitors, including lisinopril, can cause angioedema, which may involve the face, extremities, lips, tongue, glottis, or larynx. This reaction can occur at any time during treatment and is more common in Black patients. If angioedema occurs, the medication should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. Intestinal angioedema has also been reported, presenting with abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting, and resolving after stopping the ACE inhibitor. Patients undergoing desensitization therapy (e.g., for hymenoptera venom) or dialysis with high-flux membranes while on ACE inhibitors may experience life-threatening anaphylactoid reactions. In such cases, alternative therapies or dialysis membranes should be considered. Excessive hypotension is rare in uncomplicated hypertensive patients but may occur in those who are volumeor salt-depleted, such as those on diuretics or dialysis. Therapy should be initiated under close medical supervision, especially in patients with severe heart failure or ischemic heart disease, as excessive blood pressure reduction could lead to myocardial infarction or stroke. Lisinopril has been associated with rare cases of agranulocytosis, particularly in patients with renal impairment or collagen vascular disease. Periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts is recommended in such patients. ACE inhibitors can cause a syndrome starting with cholestatic jaundice or hepatitis, progressing to fulminant hepatic necrosis, and sometimes death. Patients developing jaundice or significant liver enzyme elevations should discontinue the medication and receive appropriate follow-up. Use of drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy can harm the fetus, leading to reduced renal function, oligohydramnios, lung hypoplasia, skeletal deformities, and neonatal complications such as anuria and death. If pregnancy is detected, the medication should be discontinued immediately. Hydrochlorothiazide can cause acute transient myopia and acute angle-closure glaucoma, typically within hours to weeks of initiation. Symptoms include decreased visual acuity and ocular pain. If untreated, this can lead to permanent vision loss. Prompt discontinuation of the drug and appropriate medical or surgical intervention are necessary. Thiazides, including hydrochlorothiazide, may cause electrolyte imbalances such as hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and hypomagnesemia. They may also precipitate hyperuricemia or gout and unmask latent diabetes mellitus. Periodic monitoring of serum electrolytes is recommended, especially in patients with excessive vomiting or receiving parenteral fluids. Adverse reactions reported with lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide include dizziness, cough, fatigue, muscle cramps, and orthostatic hypotension. These effects are generally mild and transient but may require dose adjustments or discontinuation in some cases.
